transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
>> Live from NPR News in New York City,
I'm Dua Leisai Kowtow.
The White House has, again, shut out CNN from the video pool
of five networks that share the cost and logistics
of covering the president.
But this is the first since CNN won a court ruling a few days
ago over access to the White House.
The Justice Department is appealing.
>> As NPR's David full conflict reports.
>> CNN and MS Now and Politico sued after President Trump
ordered their journalists be barred from the White House
because he thought they were too negative.
A federal judge ruled that ban was likely unconstitutional
and put it on hold until trial.
The pool is a different matter.
It's made up of ABC, CBS, Fox News, and NBC, as well as CNN.
The networks are refusing to take CNN's turn in the rotation.
There was no major TV pool coverage at the White House
Friday and will be none of Trump's time in Florida
this weekend in smaller spaces
where the full press cannot attend.
The Justice Department is investigating the pool networks
saying their consultation over CNN's missed turn
may constitute illegal antitrust behavior.
David full conflict, NPR News.
>> Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky says
the disruptions on SpaceX's military-grade version
of Starlink are hindering Ukraine's efforts
to intercept Russia's jet-powered drones
from Kyiv, NPR's Joanne Kekiss's reports.
>> Ukraine's military uses star shield terminals
to help defend cities from Russia's jet-powered drones
and to assist soldiers on the front line.
Units first noticed speed caps on star shield on October 14th.
Speaking to reporters on WhatsApp, Zelensky said today
that those caps remain in place.
Regarding Starlink and star shield,
we are talking about this on the military level, Zelensky said.
On the diplomatic level,
we are also reaching out to everyone,
including SpaceX.
No one is responding right now.
Elon Musk, who owns SpaceX,
says the White House ultimately controls star shield.
President Trump claims he did not order
the restrictions on Ukraine.
Joanne Kekiss's NPR News, Kyiv.
>> It was a mixed week on Wall Street
as inflation continues to cause headaches.
NPR's Scott Horsley reports blue chips were up for the week,
but the broader market was down.
>> Reports this week from the Labor Department
showed prices climbing faster
than forecasters expected in September.
Inflation's been outpacing wage gains in recent months,
but shoppers continue to open their wallets.
The National Retail Federation says it expects holiday sales
to grow more than 4% this year to just over a trillion dollars.
On Friday, the Treasury Department said
the federal deficit for the just-ended fiscal year
was nearly $2 trillion.
The government's borrowing so much money,
it's putting upward pressure on interest rates for everyone else.
For the week, the Dow Jones Industrial Average
rose 2/3 of a percent,
but the S&P 500 index fell nearly 2%,
and the NASDAQ tumbled 4.5%.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
>> This is "NPR News" from New York.
People with a certain gene variant
have a higher risk of developing Alzheimer's disease.
NPR's Ping Huang reports it may have to do
with how their brain cells respond to stress.
>> The APOE gene helps transport lipids,
which are tiny globules of fat, through the brain.
Many Alzheimer's patients have a variant called APOE4,
which seems to cause malfunction in some people's brain cells.
Lipids accumulate as droplets
instead of forming a protective sheath around the cell's axons.
Researchers at MIT have started to figure out how that happens.
Leila Akai, lead author on a new study,
says it's typically a stress response.
>> This can happen in response to too many nutrients,
to having not enough nutrients,
to thermal cues, other kinds of stressful cues.
>> Akai and her colleagues conducted experiments
on lab-grown human brain cells and mice.
They found that manipulating a key enzyme
could reverse the damage,
offering a potential target for future Alzheimer's treatments.
The paper is published in the journal "Cell Stem Cell."
Ping Huang, NPR News.
>> In Bent, Oregon, carnations, sunflowers, stuffed animals,
and candles are lying on the sidewalk today
in front of Silver Rail Elementary.
That's where three children and their teacher
were killed by a 16-year-old shooter just two days ago.
A 7-year-old and another teacher were also wounded.
Local resident Marissa Hurley told the Oregonian
that she helped organize a candlelight vigil last night,
attended by several hundred people,
because she said she felt helpless
and needed to do something actionable.
I'm Duwah Lee Saikowtow, NPR News, in New York City.

topics.text: White House again bars CNN from press pool, days after court ruling favoring CNN
Ukraine's Zelensky says SpaceX Starlink speed caps are hindering drone interception efforts
Wall Street mixed for the week as inflation rises faster than expected in September
Study finds APOE4 gene variant may disrupt brain cell lipid handling in Alzheimer's risk
Oregon community holds vigil at Silver Rail Elementary after shooting killed three children, teacher
